entry.evidence: The results of these two methods are compared to verify the feasibility and accuracy of using dense seismic array data with an airgun source

steps.action: Cite prior characterization of large-volume airgun sources as repeatable, efficient sources rich in S-wave phases, with signals that can be stacked to raise SNR.
steps.quote: airgun sources are characterized by high signal repeatability, a high energy conversion efficiency, and abundant seismic phases

steps.action: Cite the Yamaoka (ACROSS) amplitude-distance method, the Aki coda normalization method, and Su et al.'s Hutubi airgun attenuation study as the methodological precedent.
steps.quote: demonstrated the feasibility of using artificial seismic sources to study the attenuation characteristics of the subsurface

steps.action: State the aim: test whether a dense array with an airgun source yields reliable shallow Qs^-1, by checking whether two methods give consistent results.
steps.quote: The results of these two methods are compared to verify the feasibility and accuracy

steps.action: Set up the two forward models (geometric spreading plus exp(-bx) amplitude-distance decay; S-to-coda spectral ratio vs distance). Drop the radiation-pattern term as an auxiliary, on the basis of Jiang's (2017) finding that the airgun is isotropic.
steps.quote: Therefore, we ignore the influence of the airgun source radiation pattern on the source spectrum

steps.action: Select 37 evenly distributed EPS stations (2.3–23.4 km epicentral distance) from the 380-station Binchuan array deployed in 2017. Linearly stack 215–1073 shots per station.
steps.quote: Since this is a feasibility study, we selected 37 stations from this dense array for calculation

steps.action: Check the stacking premise by comparing waveforms before and after stacking at station 026, the station with the fewest shots.
steps.quote: The SNR is significantly improved after stacking, indicating that the poststack waveforms can be used for subsequent research.

steps.action: Filter the stacked data at 1–20 Hz and pick P and S arrivals manually, finding an S apparent velocity of about 3.3 km/s. Restrict the analysis to S waves.
steps.quote: Thus, this study uses only S waves for the calculation.

steps.action: Trace ray paths (maximum penetration about 4 km) through the Chen et al. (2016) 1-D model to obtain an average S-wave velocity of 2.87 km/s, used in both methods.
steps.quote: we calculated that the average S-wave velocity over 4 km was approximately 2.87 km/s

steps.action: Fix the processing choices. Amplitude-distance: 8-s S window, RMS spectrum at 2–6 Hz, weighted mean frequency. Coda: Butterworth bands at 2–6 Hz, coda window at tc = 17 s, near stations reduced to 17 s with a master decay curve (Table 1).
steps.quote: For that purpose, we made a master curve for the decay of coda amplitude against lapse time

steps.action: Check the premise that the selected window is coda: test linear decay of ln[A/K] against lapse time, as predicted by Sato's single isotropic scattering model, at three stations (Fig. 7).
steps.quote: it is necessary to check whether the selected signal is a coda wave after determining the signal window

steps.action: Fit the amplitude-distance decay to obtain Qs^-1 = 0.0260 ± 0.0103 (EW), 0.0264 ± 0.0109 (NS) and 0.0256 ± 0.0080 (UD) at a mean frequency of about 3.6 Hz. Station 97 is noted as an outlier.
steps.quote: the curve of the amplitude spectrum versus distance was obtained by fitting (Fig. 8)

steps.action: Compare the estimates across the three components. EW and NS agree, which justifies using the EW component only.
steps.quote: value of EW component is almost equal to the value of NS component

steps.action: Regress the coda-normalized amplitudes against distance in five bands: Qs^-1 falls from 0.0365 ± 0.0205 at 2 Hz to 0.0186 ± 0.0070 at 6 Hz. Fit the power law Qs^-1(f) ≈ 0.0554 f^-0.5643.
steps.quote: least-squares line were fitted to the data in all frequency bands

steps.action: Evaluate the coda power law at 3.6 Hz (0.0269) and compare it with the amplitude-distance value (0.0260). The two are declared consistent.
steps.quote: values calculated by the Yamaoka amplitude–distance attenuation method and the Aki coda normalization method are consistent

steps.action: Remove the outliers and refit. Dropping station 97 in the amplitude-distance method gives 0.0221 ± 0.0094 (15% change). Dropping five coda outliers changes the estimates by 1.9–7.5% and gives 0.0581 f^-0.5668.
steps.quote: station No. 97 was eliminated, and the fit was performed again to obtain a new amplitude attenuation curve (Fig. 10)

steps.action: Refine the methodological claim: coda normalization is more stable than amplitude-distance. Recommend high-precision data and dividing areas with different sediment thickness or topography.
steps.quote: the Yamaoka amplitude–distance attenuation method is relatively unstable

steps.action: Map the anomalous stations of both methods against topography and sediment thickness (Figs. 13–15).
steps.quote: are emphasized in Fig. 14 to explore the relationship between the anomalous spectral amplitudes and the topography

steps.action: Propose explanations for the anomalous stations: a basin-edge effect, basin amplification at the depocenter, a conversion error at station 138, local site factors, and weak attenuation in the hard hilly terrain.
steps.quote: the amplitude is larger than the fitted curve due to the basin edge effect

steps.action: Compute the basin resonance frequency from fR = vs/4m (350 m of sediment, vs = 500 m/s) to test the amplification rival against the 2 Hz anomaly.
steps.quote: the resonance frequency in the basin is approximately 0.36 Hz based on Eq. 16

steps.action: Exclude basin amplification for stations 56 and 120, because 0.36 Hz differs from the anomalous 2 Hz band.
steps.quote: The influence of the basin amplification effect can be excluded.

steps.action: Retain local site factors (depocenter stations) and weak attenuation of the hilly area (stations 131, 66) as speculative explanations, pending site data and the full array.
steps.quote: we speculate that the local site factors may be the cause of the deviation

steps.action: Compare the Qs^-1 law with published estimates and with the Zhang et al. (2020) low shallow velocities. The published estimates are Yunnan natural-earthquake coda (Wang et al. 2005), Kanto, Kagoshima, the Satoh (2006) rock-type models and the North China Basin boreholes. The value lies between hard soil and sedimentary rock, close to North China.
steps.quote: These comparisons further demonstrate the rationality and accuracy of the results of this study.

steps.action: Keep the claim that a dense array with an airgun source can measure shallow-media Qs^-1, with stable results consistent between the two methods.
steps.quote: a comparison of the calculation results of the two methods confirms that an airgun seismic source can be used to detect the

No; Qs^-1 is inferred by fitting two forward models to stacked amplitudes

No rival to the main claim; rivals only for the anomalous stations (edge effect, basin amplification, site factors, hard hilly terrain)
Basin resonance at 0.36 Hz versus the 2 Hz anomaly separates amplification from the other explanations

Kept: the two methods are consistent, so the capability is judged feasible

end.claim: A dense seismic array with a large-volume airgun source can estimate shallow-media Qs^-1. The amplitude-distance (0.0260 ± 0.0103) and coda normalization (0.0269 at 3.6 Hz from 0.0554 f^-0.5643) methods agree, and the coda method is more stable.

decisive_move.sentence: The feasibility claim rests on comparing the two independent analyses of the same stacked records (0.0260 vs 0.0269 at 3.6 Hz); without this comparison there is only an estimate, not a characterized capability.

gates.evidence: The data were collected in an earlier experiment imaging the Binchuan basin with active sources (Acknowledgements, p. 18); this paper only selects 37 stations from it. The two methods could have disagreed, but no agreement threshold was set. The fit uncertainties are large (about 40% of the value), and agreement is asserted after noting that 'the calculation of the Q value is volatile' (§4.2 ¶1). Nothing was fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: least-squares linear regression for Q estimation

limits:
No review file was supplied, so the review sequence is not coded, although the acknowledgements say two reviewers improved the paper.

Coding choices:
- Coding the array deployment as part of an observation step (rather than inherited or cited) is an inference: the array was deployed in 2017 by the authors' institute for basin imaging.
- Composition capability_first is a best fit by inference. The walk is a feasibility check of a source-array combination by agreement between two methods. It has no exploration phase and the question is posed at the start, so it only loosely matches the listed definition.

What the paper does not show:
- There is no quantitative agreement criterion. The two estimates overlap within large fitting errors, and 'consistent' is asserted.
- The fixed velocity of 2.87 km/s and the radiation-pattern assumption are not varied. The sensitivity of Q to them is not reported.
- Only one source location and 37 of 380 stations are used; no held-out stations are tested.
- The paper makes no explicit 'first' claims; it states only that little research exists on airgun coda waves (§3.2 ¶2).

Sub-claims at other statuses:
- Frequency-dependent law Qs^-1 ≈ 0.0554 f^-0.5643: estimate_with_resolution (§4.2 ¶1).
- Coda normalization more stable than amplitude-distance: best_explanation, based on the outlier-removal tests (§5.1 ¶3).
- Anomalous stations due to basin edge effect, local site factors and hard hilly terrain: best_explanation, explicitly speculative, with basin amplification excluded by the resonance calculation (§5.2 ¶2–3).
- Binchuan Qs^-1 between hard soil and sedimentary rock, similar to the North China Basin: a comparison-based claim, not tested (§5.3 ¶2).
